title: Eggs Benedict
subtitle: Poached eggs and Canadian bacon on an English muffin with hollandaise
excerpt: Eggs Benedict is a classic American brunch dish of poached eggs and sliced cooked ham on toasted English muffins, topped with hollandaise sauce. The hollandaise is the most technically demanding part: an emulsified butter sauce stabilised with egg yolks and lemon juice.
sourceNotes: Eggs Benedict is attributed to various New York establishments of the late 19th century. Delmonico's restaurant in New York and the Waldorf Hotel are both cited as originators. The dish became a staple of American hotel brunch service and spread worldwide.

content.text: Eggs Benedict has two components that need coordinating: the hollandaise sauce and the poached eggs. Make the hollandaise first, keep it warm over a bain-marie at a very low temperature, then poach the eggs. Both the sauce and the eggs must be hot at the same moment. The hollandaise can be held for up to 30 minutes without much degradation.

items.prepNote: 8 whole for poaching, 4 yolks for hollandaise

content.text: Put the 4 egg yolks and 2 tablespoons of cold water in a heatproof bowl. Set over a pan of barely simmering water (the bowl must not touch the water). Whisk vigorously for 3 to 4 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and tripled in volume, and leaves a trail when you lift the whisk.

Remove from the heat. Very slowly pour in the melted butter in a thin steady stream, whisking constantly. Start with drops, then increase to a thin trickle. If you add the butter too fast, the sauce will split. Season with salt, white pepper, and lemon juice. Keep warm over very low heat, stirring occasionally.

Bring a deep pan of water to a gentle simmer (not boiling). Add the vinegar. Crack each egg into a small cup. Create a gentle swirl in the water with a spoon. Slide one egg at a time into the centre of the swirl. Poach for 3 minutes for a runny yolk. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.

Toast the English muffins. Top each half with sliced ham. Place a poached egg on each muffin half. Spoon the hollandaise generously over the top. Finish with a grind of black pepper and, if you like, a pinch of cayenne.

items.symptom: Hollandaise has split into oily lumps
items.cause: Butter was added too quickly, or the sauce overheated
items.fix: Start again with a new yolk in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it as if it were the butter. Alternatively, add a spoonful of ice water and whisk vigorously: this sometimes rescues a lightly split sauce.

items.symptom: Poached eggs spread out and look ragged
items.cause: Eggs were not fresh (older whites are thinner and spread more) or water was boiling rather than gently simmering
items.fix: Use the freshest eggs possible. The water should barely tremble: vigorous boiling breaks the egg apart. The vinegar in the water helps the white coagulate faster.

content.text: Swap the ham for smoked salmon. All other elements remain the same. This version is sometimes called Eggs Royale in the UK. Add a few capers and some dill alongside the hollandaise.
